title: Unclogging the Pipeline: Why Aren’t More Workers Flocking to Lucrative Trade Jobs?
summary: By nearly every measure, trade jobs offer stability, good compensation, and satisfaction in the American economy. And yet, the workforce pipeline feeding them is fragmented, informal, and increasingly strained.
body_text: Unclogging the Pipeline: Why Aren’t More Workers Flocking to Lucrative Trade Jobs? Key takeaways The typical trade worker earns $65,000 and has high job satisfaction, yet the workforce supply chain remains highly fragmented and reliant on word-of-mouth. Half of trade workers learn on the job (50%), and 32% said they are self-taught or learned through friends and family. Job openings have spiked by up to 34% over the past year across core trade sectors like construction, manufacturing, and transportation , leaving 45% of current workers regularly handling the workload of multiple people due to understaffing. Despite rapid technological evolution, only 7.9% say automation and AI are reducing the need for their skillset . However, only 17% of workers say their employer provides extensive training on new automation tools , which may contribute to high turnover across the trades, threatening broader economic progress. By nearly every measure, trade jobs offer stability, good compensation, and satisfaction in the American economy. And yet, the workforce pipeline feeding them is fragmented, informal, and increasingly strained. Laying the foundation: High salaries and job satisfaction provide economic stability The typical trade worker in the U.S. makes $65,000 per year, according to ZipRecruiter’s comprehensive national survey of trade workers. Specialized skill sets come with even higher compensation, with skilled construction workers earning a median of $75,000 and plant operators earning $84,000. Many tradespeople start their careers debt-free (68% carry no student debt), and, combined with high salaries, this provides a solid foundation for financial stability. Unionized workers fare even better, with higher incomes stemming from increased bargaining power, but most trade workers, 75%, are ununionized, leaving them with more limited support. Trade workers often find themselves in long and satisfying careers: Just under half (49%) have been in the field for 11 or more years Over three-quarters (77%) said they would choose to go into the trades again 82% say they would recommend the trades to a younger worker; it is apparent that this career choice leads to long-term stability Workers in the trades have every reason to stick around in their positions. Public data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) shows that construction workers have been clinging tightly to their roles, with their quits rate down to 1.3% . Manufacturing follows suit with a quits rate at 1.4% , compared to the overall level of 1.9% in June. Overall, the survey shows that trade workers stay in their positions due to pay (74%), stability (46%), and benefit offerings (46%). For many, employers are meeting their needs, with over 91% of trade workers reporting a sense of belonging at work. Powering through stagnant hiring: Rising demand and automation collide with an aging workforce Demand for trade workers is high, but recent public data from the BLS shows hiring has not kept pace with job openings. This stagnant hiring signals that employers are having a difficult time finding the right talent to fill open roles. The result is current trade workers feeling more pressure to execute despite being short-staffed. According to the survey, just under half (45%) of trade workers say they regularly perform work meant for more than one person due to understaffing Nearly one in five, 18%, feels this daily Yet some trade workers are willing to step into extra work, with 35% working a second job or side hustle Younger workers are more likely to adopt a second income stream, with the share jumping to 45% The most popular side hustle is freelance work in their expert trade (38%), pointing to the increased industry demand, calling existing workers to take on additional projects An early indicator of growth on the horizon is an increase in overtime hours for manufacturing employees. Separate public data from the BLS shows an uptick in non-supervisory manufacturing overtime hours over the past three months, reaching an average of 4.1 hours per week in June, up from 3.7 hours a year ago. This indicates the industry is seeing increased demand that has yet to be absorbed by new hiring. Trade workers generally appreciate these opportunities, as 90% say they welcome the chance to take overtime when it comes. Overtime does not just boost wages; it signals growth in the industry that leads to more jobs down the road, especially in clean power generation. The BLS JOLTS report states that job openings have increased by 34% in the last year in construction and by 32% in manufacturing Growth is expected to continue as data center construction, EV charging infrastructure, and residential home demand increase According to BLS projections , skilled trades rank among the top five industries expecting the greatest employment growth between 2024 and 2034 : solar (+182%), wind (+84%), geothermal (+41%), electrical power generation (+32%), and electrical equipment manufacturing (+29%) Jobs in specialized trades, like electricians (+9%) and HVAC techs (+8%), are also set to see BLS-projected demand in excess of the overall labor market average of 3.1% The trades are aging, but young workers are showing up The challenge lies in ensuring there are enough workers to meet this increased demand. The trades have a slightly higher incidence of older workers than non-trade occupations. According to public 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) data, 13.7% of the trade workforce is 60+, compared to a similar share of 13.4% for non-trade workers. It’s notable that more than one in seven trade workers is 60+, but young workers are showing up to keep the flow of labor supply steady, for now. According to an analysis of ACS data, for every 5 older workers in the trades (60+), there are 6 young workers (aged 16 to 25) stepping in to take their place This is actually better than non-trade professions, where a slightly lower rate of 5.5 young workers enter for every 5 workers aged 60+ Trade jobs might see a higher ratio of young to old workers as many older trade workers leave their posts early due to the demanding physical toll of their jobs. In fact, 44% of trade workers state that the physical toll of their work has impacted their health. Older respondents were less likely to state that their physical health was impacted by their job than younger respondents. Only 42% of trade workers 65+ respond that their roles significantly impact their health, versus 49% of those aged 18-29. But this is likely because older respondents were more likely to hold management and office roles (16% of 65+, vs 4.9% of 18-29), which are less physically demanding overall. Many exit the workforce early , before they hit full retirement age, meaning this population is especially vulnerable to financial distress as they are unable to tap key retirement benefits before they hit their physical limits. Some have called for additional retirement benefits or expanded workplace programs to support the aging trade workforce. The significant aging of this key workforce demographic warrants an intentional approach to ensure the young workers are supported for their careers ahead, and those aging out have a stable path ahead of them. AI and automation are changing the work, not replacing the worker As the trades become younger, with older workers aging out or retiring and young workers entering the picture, technology continues to modernize the field. Artificial intelligence and automation are already reshaping the daily lives of these professionals. A majority, 55%, of workers note that automation has changed the tools they use but has not reduced their workload , while 37% say it has actually made their job easier or safer by handling the most strenuous physical tasks Only a small minority of 7.9% express concern that technology has reduced the need for their specific skills This tech adoption is also reflected in daily habits, with 23% of trade workers reporting regular use of AI tools and another 39% using them occasionally Because these tools assist rather than replace labor, anxiety regarding technological displacement remains relatively low A wrench in the works: Fragmented career on-ramps create a labor supply bottleneck Demand for trade workers is rising, and workers themselves point to the stability and benefits of working in these industries. This should be good news to job seekers. But the on-ramp to establishing a career in the trades is fragmented at best, which could be slowing workforce growth. According to the survey, workers found their way to the trades through a disjointed, rather than centralized, path. The fact that so many trade workers are able to self-teach or learn on the job could mean that these opportunities are ripe for the picking for today’s job seekers looking for a career change, even if they lack formal training. However, the data show income levels are much lower for trade workers who say they are self-taught (a median income of $65,000) versus those who went through formal channels, like an apprenticeship ($91,000). This shows the value in having formalized credentials and highlights equity disparities caused by fragmented starting points. Apprenticeship opportunities have been rising since federal policy measures like the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) introduced targeted incentives aiming to increase formal training programs for young workers getting started in the trades. Just this July, the US Department of Labor awarded $162 million to expand registered apprenticeship programs in specialized industries. Yet, finding out about these opportunities remains a challenge, as only 14% of current trade workers completed an apprenticeship, according to the survey. Meanwhile, over half (51%) of current trade workers first learned about opportunities in the trades through friends and family, and only 16% found this path online. This disjointed on-ramp makes identifying opportunities challenging for workers, creating a bottleneck that could be limiting labor supply. Slow hiring in the trades has a deep impact across the US economy. When construction roles go unfilled, houses take longer to build, and home prices go up. When electricians are in short supply, the electrification of new data centers slows technological advancements. When heavy machinery mechanics are unavailable, vital transportation and supply chains grind to a halt, driving up the cost of everyday consumer goods. The fragmented environment leading into trade work could be slowing progress and impacting pricing across the entire market as demand for these jobs rises. Welding the gap: Lack of formal mentorship and upskilling drives turnover In such a disjointed market, the transfer of knowledge depends heavily on workers stepping up to the plate instead of relying on formal programs, much like the on-ramp to getting into trade work in the first place. Only 37% of trade workers say their employer has a formal mentorship program, according to the survey. Instead, 51% rely on informal knowledge transfer, and 9.6% have no touchpoints for expert knowledge sharing at all. Employers are also falling short on providing specific training for new advancements. The data reveals that when it comes to automation and new technology, formal training is scarce. Perhaps this lack of structural support explains why 33% of trade workers describe turnover as high or very high at their company. It is challenging to get in the door, and once there, limited opportunities to upskill formally mean workers must largely fend for themselves. Blueprint for the future: Fixing the clog in labor supply through structured training The trades offer a robust, lucrative, and highly satisfying career path for millions of Americans. However, the data clearly show that a fractured pipeline and a lack of formal upskilling are holding the industry back from its full potential. As technological advancements accelerate and infrastructure demands compound, relying on word-of-mouth recruiting and informal on-the-job training is no longer a viable strategy for the broader economy. To meet the surging demand of the next decade, industry leaders, educators, and public-sector partners can expand and simplify pathways into the trades. Three priorities consistently emerge from the data: Create clearer pathways: Centralizing and digitizing the discovery of trade programs, shifting away from a reliance on personal networks, can give high school students and career-changers more chances to find apprenticeships and vocational training programs, increasing the instance of young people entering these fields. Invest in structured upskilling: With AI and automation rapidly changing the tools of the trade, employers will increasingly need to invest in structured training rather than expect workers to adapt on their own time. Systematize knowledge sharing: Companies need to incentivize their most experienced, older workers to formally mentor the incoming generation, capturing institutional knowledge before it retires and giving older workers a clean exit path, rather than leaving them to exit early or face physical challenges on the job. By modernizing how we recruit, train, and support trade professionals, we can unclog the labor pipeline, secure the workforce needed to build our future infrastructure, and open the door to lasting financial stability for the current and next generations of American workers. Methodology The insights in this report are primarily derived from a nationally representative, comprehensive survey of 1,500 trade workers nationwide, administered by PureSpectrum between May 25 and June 11, 2026, assessing compensation, job satisfaction, entry pathways, and views on workplace technology. External labor market data, baseline employment projections, historical quits rates, and demographic ratios are cited directly within the text and sourced from public databases maintained by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS via IPUMS).

title: FEBRABAN TECH 2026: talks and tracks to follow
summary: Discover the featured speakers, panels, and tracks at FEBRABAN TECH 2026, taking place from August 24 to 26 in São Paulo.
body_text: With ten simultaneous stages and an agenda dedicated to artificial intelligence, security, infrastructure, payment methods, and new financial models, choosing what to follow at FEBRABAN TECH 2026 requires planning. Scheduled for August 24, 25, and 26 , the event will be held for the first time at Distrito Anhembi in São Paulo. This edition will feature ten simultaneous stages, workshops, and spaces for podcast recordings. The Febraban Auditorium alone will have six stages operating at the same time. With the theme “Intelligent Agents, Human Leadership” , the conference places at the center of its agenda an issue that is already part of financial institutions’ decision-making: how to expand the use of artificial intelligence without losing sight of governance, security, responsibility, and human participation. To help organize the agenda, we selected speakers, panels, and tracks related to discussions with the greatest potential impact on the strategy, technology, and operations of financial institutions. What to expect from FEBRABAN TECH 2026 Organized by the Brazilian Federation of Banks, FEBRABAN TECH brings together representatives from the financial, technology, sustainability, telecommunications, retail, and other sectors connected to the digital economy. The 2026 edition will feature 13 content tracks , including artificial intelligence agents, future engineering, digital identity, payment methods, cybersecurity , and sustainable finance. The event is also expanding its structure after welcoming 58,000 visitors in 2025. Given the extensive agenda, session choices should consider not only the prominence of the guests but also the relationship between each discussion and companies’ priorities. AI governance, security, customer experience, digital assets, and infrastructure modernization are among the topics expected to drive the industry. Talks and panels to add to your agenda The direction of innovation in the Brazilian banking industry Panel with Milton Maluhy Filho, Marcelo Noronha, Tarciana Medeiros, Carlos Vieira, and Roberto Sallouti Mon 08/24 | 10:00 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. | Febraban Auditorium The agenda brings together executives from Brazil’s largest financial institutions, including Milton Maluhy Filho, CEO of Itaú Unibanco; Marcelo Noronha, CEO of Bradesco; Tarciana Medeiros, President of Banco do Brasil; Carlos Vieira, President of Caixa; and Roberto Sallouti, CEO of BTG Pactual. The presence of these leaders provides a focused view of the strategic priorities of the Brazilian financial system. Artificial intelligence, new business models, regulation, customer experience, and competitiveness are expected to appear at different points in the discussion. As the opening panel, the session also helps identify the topics that may gain greater prominence throughout the three-day event. For executives and professionals involved in strategy, innovation, and financial products, it is a relevant session for understanding how leading institutions are interpreting the current technology cycle. Keynote – Joel Monkyr Joel Mokyr | Economic historian and winner of the 2025 Prize in Economic Sciences Mon 08/24 | 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. | Febraban Auditorium Joel Mokyr is known for his research on the conditions required for technological progress to result in sustained economic growth. The 2025 Prize in Economic Sciences recognized his contribution to understanding the requirements that allow progress through innovation to continue. His participation expands the discussion beyond the immediate applications of new tools. Rather than viewing artificial intelligence solely from the perspective of short-term productivity, his research makes it possible to discuss how knowledge, openness to new ideas, and institutional capacity influence innovation cycles. For professionals working in planning and technology investments, this historical perspective can help distinguish temporary trends from movements capable of changing economic structures and business models. Keynote – John Maeda John Maeda | Author and global reference in computational design and artificial intelligence Wed 08/26 | 10:50 a.m. to 11:40 a.m. | Febraban Auditorium John Maeda is an author, designer, and one of the leading references at the intersection of technology, human experience, and computational design. His work includes the book How to Speak Machine , dedicated to the relationship between design and digital systems. The discussion is especially relevant for financial institutions investing in artificial intelligence, automation, and digital channels. A solution may be highly technically sophisticated and still face adoption difficulties when the user experience does not keep pace with that evolution. For professionals in product, UX, digital channels, and innovation, the talk offers an opportunity to reflect on how to incorporate design from the conception of systems, rather than only at the final stage of development. Kaynote- Radia Perlman Radia Perlman | Engineer and global reference in network infrastructure Tue 08/25 | 10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. | Febraban Auditorium Known as the “mother of the internet,” Radia Perlman is an engineer and fellow at Dell Technologies. Her work played an important role in the development of the protocols and architectures that support modern networks. Her presence is particularly important at a time when financial institutions need to assess resilience, network security, distributed computing, and the potential impacts of quantum computing on current systems. Even when banking security is not the main topic, understanding infrastructure fundamentals is essential to discussing cloud, real-time processing, service availability, and the protection of financial operations. Strategic tracks for the financial industry In addition to international guests and executive panels, the agenda is organized into tracks that cover different dimensions of financial innovation. From the data center to the AI cluster: infrastructure, automation, and the new banking core Track: Resilient innovation: cloud, data centers, and the industry’s new engineering August 24 | 10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. | Febraban Auditorium – Purple The growth of artificial intelligence increases the infrastructure requirements of financial institutions. The adoption of generative models, multimodal systems, and real-time inference requires new decisions regarding computing capacity, availability, and processing location. The panel addresses alternatives such as proprietary AI clusters, public cloud, sovereign clouds, colocation, and distributed structures. For technology and architecture leaders, the session can contribute to the discussion on how to modernize the banking core without compromising security, operational continuity, and integration capacity. Real-time hyperpersonalization, from intent to impact Track: From big data to real-time intelligent banking August 24 | 10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. | Febraban Auditorium – Green Financial services personalization is beginning to move from models based solely on customer history toward approaches that combine current behavior, context, and intent. The session will discuss how banks can use data and artificial intelligence to develop interactions that are better suited to each moment in the customer journey. Possibilities include adaptive limits, personalized rates, financial stress prevention, and automated renegotiation. The panel is especially relevant for professionals in CRM, products, data, risk, credit, and customer experience. Exponential productivity: do customers and society benefit from multi-agent ecosystems? August 24 | 3:50 p.m. to 4:50 p.m. | Febraban Auditorium – Blue The panel addresses the transition from isolated assistants to ecosystems of specialized agents capable of sharing information, activating tools, auditing processes, and executing activities in real time. This progress expands automation opportunities, but it also requires new control practices. Governance, security, traceability, and the definition of responsibilities become part of decisions regarding the adoption of AI agents. For the financial industry, the discussion is important because these systems can operate in sensitive processes such as information analysis, customer service, fraud prevention, and decision-making support. Open Finance at scale: from data sharing to ecosystem orchestration Track: Open Finance: security and privacy vs. interoperability Mon 08/24 | 2:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. | Febraban Auditorium – Gray Open Finance is entering a stage in which the challenge lies not only in technical implementation but also in the ability to operate at scale. The track addresses the need to integrate different participants, data, and services in an increasingly interdependent ecosystem. Security, privacy, and interoperability appear as conditions for the system to generate value for customers and companies. The discussion is relevant to banks, fintechs, technology companies, and organizations developing products or partnerships based on authorized data sharing. The mindset of the next wave of banking technology Tue 08/25 | 11:20 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. | Febraban Auditorium The panel begins with a central question for the industry: how can artificial intelligence, quantum computing, digital identity, and new architectures be incorporated without compromising the security and stability of operations? The session offers a perspective on the technologies that may guide the next generation of banking services and on the criteria required to turn experimentation into responsible adoption. It is recommended content for professionals in strategy, innovation, architecture, security, and technology planning. A new window opens with stablecoins Track: Drex and the global race for stablecoins Wed 08/26 | 2:00 p.m. to 3:00 p.m. | Febraban Auditorium – Burgundy The session will discuss the advancement of stablecoins as infrastructure for payments, settlement, and digital financial operations. The discussion takes place at a time when the technological and privacy challenges related to Drex are being reassessed, while private digital currencies gain ground in international payments and new business models. Financial institutions should pay attention to how stablecoins can integrate with existing systems, which use cases offer the greatest potential, and which regulatory and operational requirements need to be considered. Evertec at FEBRABAN TECH 2026 Evertec will be present at FEBRABAN TECH 2026 with its own booth at Distrito Anhembi. During the three-day event, our team will be available to present end-to-end solutions for banks and financial services , covering everything from payment processing to digital platform management for institutions of all sizes across Latin America. If you are attending the event, stop by our booth. It is a great opportunity to discuss your business challenges and see firsthand what Evertec has been developing for the financial industry. The agenda is subject to change. Therefore, the dates, times, and stages of each session should be checked on the event’s official agenda before attending. Frequently asked questions about FEBRABAN TECH 2026: When will FEBRABAN TECH 2026 take place? The event will be held on August 24, 25, and 26, 2026. Where will FEBRABAN TECH 2026 be held? The event will take place at Distrito Anhembi, located at 1,209 Avenida Olavo Fontoura, in Santana, in the northern area of São Paulo. What is the theme of FEBRABAN TECH 2026? The central theme of this edition is “Intelligent Agents, Human Leadership.” The proposal is to discuss the advancement of artificial intelligence and autonomous agents without losing sight of responsibility, governance, and the appeal of people. Who are the confirmed speakers? Confirmed guests include Joel Mokyr, John Maeda, and Radia Perlman. The event will also feature leaders such as Milton Maluhy Filho, Marcelo Noronha, Tarciana Medeiros, Carlos Vieira, and Roberto Sallouti. What are the main topics of this edition? The 13 content tracks include AI agents, future engineering, digital identity, payment methods, cybersecurity, sustainable finance, and other topics related to the digital economy. How many stages will FEBRABAN TECH 2026 have? This edition will feature ten simultaneous stages. The Febraban Auditorium will have six stages operating at the same time, two more than in the previous edition. How can I get a pass? Registration is available through the official FEBRABAN TECH website . There are in-person pass options for one day or all three days of the event, with individual and group options. Access to the sessions is subject to seat availability. Will the content be available to watch after the event? The in-person pass includes access to videos of the panels made available on the FEBRABAN TECH website after the conference, in accordance with the conditions provided by the organizers
